newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa talks seen mired in budget wrangling.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa talks seen mired in budget wrangling.

text.p: Cocoa nations, gathering for London talks on Wednesday, will try to settle long-standing differences over how they should use revenues from buffer stock sales.

Three-day talks of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) will also focus on progress made in output cuts agreed in September and any fresh moves by producer members to counter possible changes in the composition of chocolate.
"It will be a low-key show," said one delegate.
Discussions will be dominated by a looming decision on how to allocate a last tranche of $330 million expected to pile up in ICCO coffers from buffer stock sales over nearly five years.
Two-thirds of the revenue from selling 250,000 tonnes of cocoa has been re-distributed to members, mainly producers, who had to pay a levy when buffer stocks were introduced in 1986.
The money was also was used in financing ICCO expenses.
The sticking point now is to find a way of allocating the last tranche while securing a steady flow of income for the organization to prevent it from curtailing activities.
A decision must be made by March.
Members have agreed to trim costs and set up a reserve fund that could secure a steady flow of interest income, but quite what should be the size of the fund remains to be decided.
"Consumers want a fund of 2.5 million sterling. We could go up to three million but that's the end for us," said Hagen Streichert, the delegate for Germany and consumers' spokesman.
Producers meanwhile are backing the ICCO executive director Eduard Kouame who favours a larger fund of some 5-6 million stg to generate more interest and hence more disposable income.
Another division is that producer countries want the ICCO to raise the necessary cash for the fund from members separately after allocating the rest of the buffer stock money.

But consumers say this could be a complicated process and say that the ICCO should simply set aside part of the buffer stock revenue to create the fund, so that it would mainly financed by producers who contributed more to the levy system.

Some countries who are still in arrears in their levy payments -the biggest debtor is Ivory Coast still owing $17.8 million to the buffer stock - should not be the ones to cash in the buffer stock profits, they said.
"It's an old fight between producers and consumers," said one delegate.
Germany will make a proposal to the ICCO executive committee for it to any the surplus money buffer stock sales for the fund.

The average price of sales since 1993 have exceeded by $37 a tonne the target price of $1,300 set by the buffer stock manager to clear the payment arrears. The surplus could total some $3 million or 1.9 million stg.

The ICCO meeting will also review an agreed cut of 90,000 tonnes in world cocoa output of some 2.5 million tonnes over the next three years which sceptical traders have said were so modest as to seem almost invisible.
Cuts were necessary to reduce world stocks to 34 percent of consumption from around 50 percent now in an effort to prevent prices from new slides in the face of huge Ivorian harvests.
"Production cuts are irrelevant unless they say how they're going to do it," said Lawrence Eagles, head of research at GNI.
Some analysts were even questioning the need to cut output at a time when global supplies are in deficit.

Producer members may discuss strategies to lobby the U.N.'s food standards committee Codex Alimentarius which will meet in June to discuss types of fat to be allowed in products labelled chocolate. It deferred a decision in its September meeting.

Cocoa growers are vehemently against the use of vegetable fats in chocolate. The European Union (EU) has yet to adopt a proposal allowing for up to five percent non-cocoa fats, a move growers say may depress cocoa demand by 200,000 tonnes a year.
